--- title: "The main types of learning" description: "Supervised, unsupervised, and where neural networks actually fit, with one dataset asked three different questions." order: 3 categories: [foundations, supervised, unsupervised] --- ## The first question to ask of a dataset The division into supervised and unsupervised learning sounds like taxonomy, the sort of thing to memorise and forget. It is not. It is the first question anyone should ask about a proposed analysis, because it is determined by *what you have*, not by what you would like. If a specialist has labelled some of your data, you are in supervised territory and your central problem is validation. If nothing is labelled, you are in unsupervised territory and your central problem is knowing whether what you found is real. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## The idea **Supervised learning** learns from examples where the answer is known. Each row has predictors and an outcome, such as a labelled image or a station with a recorded catch, and the model learns the mapping from one to the other. It splits by the kind of outcome: *regression* for a quantity, *classification* for a category. **Unsupervised learning** has no outcome column. You hand the algorithm a table of measurements and ask what structure is in it: which stations resemble each other, which variables move together. Nothing tells the algorithm what a good answer looks like, which is exactly why the results need care. **Neural networks** are the third item in most introductions, including this course's own outline, and it is worth being straight about a wrinkle there. ::: {.callout-important} ## A correction worth making early Neural networks are not a third *type of learning*. They are a family of *models*, one choice among many for the "model" slot, and they are used for supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and other things besides. The real contrast is: supervised versus unsupervised describes **what your data lets you ask**. Random forest versus neural network describes **which machine you use to answer it**. The first decision is forced by your data; the second is yours to make. Grouping them as three parallel types is common, and it quietly suggests that reaching for a neural network is a different kind of science. It is not. ::: There is a genuine third paradigm, **reinforcement learning**, where an agent learns from the consequences of its actions. It is central to robotics and appears in marine science mainly in autonomous vehicle path planning. It is out of scope here. ## Worked example One dataset, three questions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75, strata = present) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) ``` ::: ### Supervised, regression: *how many?* The outcome is a count, so this is regression. This is the model from [the first page](what-is-machine-learning.qmd), so we will not repeat it. The outcome was that predicting abundance from environment is hard, and neither method did well. ### Supervised, classification: *is it here at all?* The outcome is now a category: present or absent. Same predictors, same forest, one changed line: `set_mode("classification")`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} outcome <- present ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate rf_class <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("classification") |> fit(outcome, data = train) predictions <- augment(rf_class, test) predictions |> accuracy(truth = present, estimate = .pred_class) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.metric |.estimator | .estimate| |:--------|:----------|---------:| |accuracy |binary | 0.785|
::: ::: Seventy-nine per cent accurate. That sounds respectable. Hold that thought. ### Unsupervised: *what kinds of station are there?* Now we remove the outcome entirely. No abundance, no presence, only the water properties. The algorithm is asked to sort 800 stations into three groups, with no notion of what makes a group good. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cluster_recipe <- recipe(~ depth_m + temperature_c + salinity_psu + chlorophyll_mg_m3, data = survey) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) clusters <- workflow() |> add_recipe(cluster_recipe) |> add_model(k_means(num_clusters = 3) |> set_engine("stats")) |> fit(survey) clustered <- bind_cols(survey, extract_cluster_assignment(clusters)) ``` ::: Normalising first is not optional. Depth ranges over hundreds of metres and temperature over about fourteen degrees; without rescaling, the clustering would be almost entirely about depth. [Section 2](../02-marine-data/index.qmd) returns to this. What did it find? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clustered |> group_by(.cluster) |> summarise( stations = n(), `depth (m)` = round(mean(depth_m)), `temp (°C)` = round(mean(temperature_c), 1), `chl (mg m⁻³)` = round(mean(chlorophyll_mg_m3), 2), `mean abundance` = round(mean(abundance), 2) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.cluster | stations| depth (m)| temp (°C)| chl (mg m⁻³)| mean abundance| |:---------|--------:|---------:|---------:|------------:|--------------:| |Cluster_1 | 364| 61| 10.2| 1.24| 4.25| |Cluster_2 | 373| 124| 7.0| 0.83| 2.86| |Cluster_3 | 63| 54| 9.2| 5.53| 7.94|
::: ::: Three recognisable habitats: a deep cold one, a shallow warm one, and a shallow productive one with three times the chlorophyll. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} labels <- c(Cluster_1 = "Shallow, warm", Cluster_2 = "Deep, cold", Cluster_3 = "Shallow, productive") clustered <- clustered |> mutate(habitat = labels[as.character(.cluster)]) p_space <- ggplot(clustered, aes(depth_m, chlorophyll_mg_m3, colour = habitat)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Chlorophyll (mg m⁻³, log scale)", colour = NULL, title = "What the algorithm was given") p_abund <- ggplot(clustered, aes(habitat, abundance, fill = habitat)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.3) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 20)) + guides(fill = "none") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Abundance", title = "What it was never told") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1)) p_space + p_abund + plot_layout(widths = c(1.25, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: stations in depth–chlorophyll space, coloured by the cluster k-means assigned. Right: abundance in each cluster. The clustering never saw abundance, yet the productive shallow cluster holds roughly twice as many individuals as the other two.](types-of-learning_files/figure-html/fig-clusters-1.png){#fig-clusters fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel is a scatter plot of chlorophyll on a logarithmic scale against depth, with points coloured into three clusters: deep and cold on the right, shallow and warm at lower chlorophyll, and shallow and productive at high chlorophyll. The right panel is a boxplot of abundance for each of the three clusters; the shallow productive cluster has a visibly higher median and a longer upper tail than the other two.' width=1700} ::: ::: One caution about that left panel: the clusters were formed in four dimensions, and any two-dimensional view of them is a shadow. Plot temperature instead of chlorophyll and the productive cluster looks scattered rather than distinct, not because the clustering is poor, but because the variable separating it is not on the axes. Judging clusters from a convenient 2-D plot is a reliable way to fool yourself, and [section 8](../08-unsupervised-learning/index.qmd) deals with it properly. This is unsupervised learning working well. Given only water properties, it recovered groupings that turn out to matter ecologically. It is also unsupervised learning at its most seductive, and [section 8](../08-unsupervised-learning/index.qmd) explains why: run it with `num_clusters = 6` and you get six equally confident habitats. ## Putting the accuracy in context Return to that 79 per cent accuracy, and compare it with the laziest possible model: always answer "present". ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions |> count(present) |> mutate(proportion = round(n / sum(n), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|present | n| proportion| |:-------|---:|----------:| |yes | 155| 0.775| |no | 45| 0.225|
::: ::: The species is present at about 78 per cent of test stations. A model that ignores every measurement and answers "present" every time scores 78 per cent. Our forest, with five environmental predictors and 500 trees, scored 79. Look at what it is actually doing: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions |> conf_mat(truth = present, estimate = .pred_class) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Truth #> Prediction yes no #> yes 146 34 #> no 9 11 ``` ::: ::: It almost never predicts absence. Of the genuinely absent stations it catches a handful and misses most. If you are mapping where the species *is not*, which is the usual reason for modelling absence, this model is close to useless, and its headline accuracy conceals that completely. This is the imbalance trap from [the previous page](applications-in-marine-science.qmd), reproduced in eight lines of code. It is the single most common way marine classification results are oversold, and it takes one comparison to catch: **always check your accuracy against the always-guess-the-common-class baseline.** [Section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) covers the measures that do not have this weakness. Curiously, a small neural network does somewhat better here on the same data, not because networks are more powerful in any general sense, but because this particular one, penalised and normalised, happened to suit the problem. That is the lesson of [section 9](../09-neural-networks/index.qmd) in advance: the network is another model, not another category of insight. ## Limits of the three-way division **"Unsupervised" does not mean "assumption-free".** Choosing k-means, choosing three clusters, choosing which variables to include and how to scale them. Every one of those is a modelling decision that shapes the answer. **Labels are often less solid than they look.** Two specialists annotating the same imagery disagree more than most people expect. A supervised model can never be more reliable than its labels, and its ceiling is the agreement rate between annotators. **The boundary is blurry in practice.** Semi-supervised learning uses a few labels and much unlabelled data; self-supervised learning manufactures labels from the data's own structure; the gap-filling task on the previous page is exactly this. The clean division is a teaching device, not a law. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Supervised or unsupervised is decided by your data, not your preference: do you have labelled examples or not? - Supervised splits by outcome type: regression for a quantity, classification for a category. In tidymodels that is one argument, `set_mode()`. - Neural networks are a *model*, not a type of learning. Choosing one is a choice of machine, not a different kind of science. - Unsupervised methods will always return groups. Finding structure is not evidence that structure exists. - Always compare classification accuracy with the always-guess-the-common-class baseline. Here, five predictors and 500 trees beat that baseline by one point. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Refit the clustering with `num_clusters = 6`, then with `num_clusters = 2`. Do the habitats still look convincing? What would make you believe one answer over another? 2. Use `sensitivity()` and `specificity()` on `predictions` in place of `accuracy()`. Which one collapses, and does that match what the confusion matrix showed?
